name: Mona Lisa
description: A portrait of the Florentine lady Lisa Gherardini that Leonardo da Vinci painted and reworked over many years, never parting with it to the end of his life. Its worldwide fame rests on that enigmatic half-smile and on the soft smoky handling of paint known as sfumato.
fact: The painting was stolen from the Louvre in 1911, and it was that theft which made it the most recognisable work of art in the world.

name: The Last Supper
description: Painted on the wall of a monastery refectory, the mural shows the moment when Christ tells the apostles that one of them will betray him. Leonardo caught the confusion and the feeling of each of the twelve disciples in the instant those words are spoken.
fact: Leonardo used tempera on dry plaster, unusual for the time, which is why the mural began to flake even in his own lifetime.

name: The Starry Night
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Vincent van Gogh painted this looking out at the pre-dawn sky from the window of the psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy. The churning spirals of cloud and the enormous stars above a sleeping village became one of the most recognisable images in the history of painting.
fact: The landscape is largely invented: the village with its pointed church spire recalls the painter's native Holland more than Provence.

name: Sunflowers
description: Van Gogh made a whole series of sunflower still lifes in yellows and ochres while preparing for the arrival of his friend Paul Gauguin in Arles. Thick loaded brushwork and an almost single-colour range make a simple bouquet extraordinarily alive.
fact: The artist painted several versions of the sunflowers, some of which now hang in museums in London, Amsterdam, Munich and Tokyo.

name: The Scream
description: The figure with the contorted face on a bridge beneath a blood-red evening sky became the emblem of existential dread. Munch said the image came to him during a walk, when he suddenly felt as though an endless scream were passing through nature itself.
fact: Munch made several versions of The Scream in different media, pastel and lithography among them.

name: Guernica
description: Picasso's enormous monochrome canvas is his response to the bombing of the Basque town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. Distorted human and animal figures convey the chaos and suffering of civilians under the bombs.
fact: It was painted in a matter of weeks specifically for the Spanish pavilion at the 1937 World's Fair in Paris.

name: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Five nude figures with angular bodies and masks in place of faces shocked Picasso's contemporaries, his closest friends included. The work is taken as the first step towards cubism and one of the great turning points of twentieth-century art.
fact: The title was not Picasso's own but a friend's: the painter first called it something else, alluding to a brothel.

name: The Persistence of Memory
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Melting pocket watches draped over a desert landscape became one of the most recognisable images in surrealism. Dalí said the idea came to him as he looked at a piece of camembert going soft in the sun.
fact: For all its huge fame the painting itself is tiny, roughly the size of a sheet of writing paper.

name: Girl with a Pearl Earring
description: A mysterious girl in a turban glancing back over her shoulder is one of the defining images of the Dutch golden age. Soft light and the large pearl earring make the picture feel like a caught moment rather than a posed portrait.
fact: Nothing is reliably known about who the girl was or what she was to Vermeer, which has bred any number of legends and fictions.

name: The Night Watch
description: This huge group canvas shows a company of Amsterdam militiamen at the moment of setting out, flooded with sharp light and deep shadow. Rembrandt broke with the conventions of the static group portrait and turned the picture into a scene in motion.
fact: The name The Night Watch came later: darkened varnish and soot led viewers for a long time to mistake a daytime scene for a nocturnal one.

name: The Birth of Venus
description: The goddess of love and beauty rises from the sea foam on a great shell while the winds blow her towards the shore. Flowing outlines and the near weightless figure of Venus made the painting one of the emblems of the Renaissance.
fact: It was painted not in oil but in tempera on canvas, which was rare for large works at the time.

name: Primavera
description: This allegory gathers almost a dozen mythological figures onto one canvas, from Venus and the Graces to Flora and Zephyrus, in a flowering orange grove. What the scene actually means is still argued over by art historians.
fact: The plants are painted so precisely that botanists can identify dozens of specific flowers and herbs.

name: The Creation of Adam
description: This section of the Sistine Chapel ceiling shows the moment God reaches out to Adam and breathes life into him. The two fingers that almost touch have become one of the most quoted gestures in all of art.
fact: Contrary to the popular legend, Michelangelo painted the ceiling not lying on his back but standing on scaffolding with his head tipped back.

name: Sistine Madonna
description: The Madonna comes down towards the viewer through parted curtains with the Christ child in her arms, while at her feet two pensive cherubs lean on the frame. Those two cherubs became one of the most endlessly reproduced images in the history of painting.
fact: The picture was painted for the altar of a monastery church in Piacenza and only reached Dresden more than two centuries later.

name: The School of Athens
description: The fresco assembles the greatest philosophers and scholars of antiquity under the vaults of a classical building, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre. Raphael gave many of them the features of his own contemporaries, Leonardo da Vinci and himself included.
fact: Raphael added the brooding Heraclitus in the foreground later, inspired by Michelangelo's work in the Sistine Chapel next door.

name: Lady with an Ermine
description: The portrait shows Cecilia Gallerani, the young favourite of the Milanese duke Ludovico Sforza, with a white ermine in her arms. The animal does more than fill out the composition: it stood for purity and played on the duke's own name.
fact: This is one of only four portraits of women securely attributed to Leonardo da Vinci that have come down to us.

name: The Garden of Earthly Delights
description: This vast triptych runs from a paradise full of strange pleasures to a hell of phantasmagorical punishments for the sinners. Its intricate hybrid creatures and dreamlike inventions have been astonishing viewers for more than five hundred years.
fact: The meaning of many details in the triptych still eludes art historians and keeps the argument over its real intention alive.

name: The Tower of Babel
description: A gigantic unfinished tower, not unlike the Roman Colosseum, rises above a medieval town and into the clouds. Bruegel treated the biblical story of human pride with astonishing architectural detail.
fact: Bruegel painted at least two versions of the Tower of Babel; the Vienna one is the larger and the better known.

name: Hunters in the Snow
description: Tired hunters and their dogs trudge back towards a snowbound village while below them the locals skate on frozen ponds. The picture belongs to a cycle on the seasons and counts as one of the first true winter landscapes in European art.
fact: The painting is part of a series of six canvases on the seasons, of which only five survive.

name: The Arnolfini Portrait
description: An Italian merchant and his wife stand in a richly furnished room, and in the convex mirror behind them the whole scene is reflected, the painter himself among it. The smallest details of the interior are set down with almost photographic exactness.
fact: Above the mirror Jan van Eyck wrote "Jan van Eyck was here", turning the painting into a kind of legal witness.

name: Las Meninas
description: Velázquez painted himself at work on a huge canvas beside the little Infanta Margarita and her maids of honour, while in a mirror at the back of the room the king and queen appear. The intricate play of gazes and space has made this one of the most studied paintings in history.
fact: Art historians still argue about what exactly Velázquez is painting on the canvas whose back is turned to us.

name: Saturn Devouring His Son
description: One of the Black Paintings that Goya made directly on the walls of his own house in the last bleak years of his life. The terrifying image of the ancient god eating his own child carries the painter's despair at violence and madness.
fact: The work was only transferred from Goya's wall onto canvas in the later nineteenth century, decades after his death.

name: The Third of May 1808
description: The painting shows French soldiers shooting Madrid rebels after the rising against Napoleon's occupation. The man in the white shirt with his arms flung up under the lantern became one of the most powerful anti-war images ever painted.
fact: Goya painted it on a commission from the Spanish government after the French had been driven out, working from memory of what he had lived through.

name: The Nude Maja
description: A naked woman poses serenely on a couch, looking straight out at the viewer, which in its own day was a bold breach of decency. The painting has an almost identical clothed counterpart, The Clothed Maja.
fact: Because of how frank the image was, the painting spent a long time in closed collections out of the public's reach.

name: Liberty Leading the People
description: A woman carrying the French flag leads the risen Parisians across the barricades during the July Revolution of 1830. The half-naked allegorical figure of Liberty became one of the great emblems of revolutionary France.
fact: The man in the top hat with a musket is thought to be Delacroix himself, and the boy with the pistols helped inspire Hugo's Gavroche.

name: The Raft of the Medusa
description: This enormous canvas shows the survivors of the wreck of the frigate Méduse, abandoned on a makeshift raft in the open ocean. Géricault worked from a real disaster that had become a loud political scandal in France.
fact: While preparing the work, Géricault studied corpses in the morgue and talked to men who had actually survived the raft.

name: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
description: A lone figure in a dark coat stands with his back to us on a crag, looking out over an endless sea of cloud among mountain peaks. The painting became one of the great emblems of Romanticism and of human contemplation before nature.
fact: Friedrich often painted his figures from behind, a device that lets the viewer stand in the wanderer's place and see the view through his eyes.
wiki_en: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog

name: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
description: A gigantic wave hangs over fishing boats while far off in the distance a tiny Mount Fuji appears. This print from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji became one of the most recognisable works of Japanese art anywhere in the world.
fact: The print was run off in thousands of copies as affordable popular art, not as a one-off work.

name: Impression, Sunrise
description: A blurred orange disc of sun over the harbour at Le Havre, painted in quick free strokes, gave a whole movement in art its name. A critic who saw the picture at the exhibition mockingly called the painters impressionists, and the term was born.
fact: In 1985 the painting was stolen from the museum and was not recovered for five years.

name: Water Lilies
meta: Musée de l'Orangerie and other collections
description: In the last decades of his life Monet barely left his garden at Giverny, painting the lily pond again and again at different hours and seasons. This immense series of several hundred canvases was the summit of his search for light and colour.
fact: Two oval rooms were built for the great panels of the series at the Orangerie in Paris, where the canvases wrap right around the viewer.

name: The Luncheon on the Grass
description: A naked woman sits at ease at a picnic in the company of fully dressed men, a combination that scandalised the public at the Paris Salon. The free handling of paint and the audacious subject made the picture one of the first challenges to academic painting.
fact: The Salon's official jury rejected the painting, and it was first shown at the notorious Salon des Refusés.

name: Olympia
description: A naked woman looks out at the viewer with a direct, almost challenging gaze while a maid brings her flowers. A plain quotation of the classical Venuses of the old masters, recast in frankly modern and realistic terms, caused an outright scandal.
fact: At the exhibition the painting had to be guarded against angry visitors who tried to damage it.

name: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette
description: A crowd of Parisians dances and enjoys itself under dappled sunlight at a popular open-air dance hall in Montmartre. Renoir caught the living atmosphere of the party through the flickering play of light and shade on faces and clothes.
fact: Renoir painted the picture on the spot, and many of the figures were modelled by his fellow painters and friends.
wiki_en: Bal du moulin de la Galette

name: Blue Dancers
description: Four young ballerinas in blue tutus adjust their costumes in the wings, seen as if in passing and from an unfamiliar angle. Degas built that sense of a snapshot largely under the influence of photography, still a new medium at the time.
fact: Degas rarely painted performances themselves, preferring backstage moments of preparation and rest.

name: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
description: Parisians take their leisure on the bank of the Seine, rendered in thousands of tiny dots of colour by the technique of pointillism. Seurat worked on this vast canvas for several years, thinking through the placement of every single figure.
fact: Seen close up, the individual figures dissolve into a mosaic of pure dots of colour.
wiki_en: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte

name: Café Terrace at Night
description: The brightly lit terrace of a café in Arles against a deep blue starry sky was one of van Gogh's first experiments with night landscapes. He painted it outdoors at night, working by the light of the gas lamps.
fact: Van Gogh was proud of having painted a night scene with no black paint at all, using only blues, greens and yellows.

name: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe
description: Van Gogh painted himself shortly after the famous episode of mental breakdown in which he injured his own ear. The calm, almost detached expression on his face sits strangely against the dramatic story behind the picture.
fact: Van Gogh made several self-portraits after that incident, documenting his own condition through painting.
wiki_en: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe

name: The Kiss
description: A couple locked in an embrace at the edge of a flowering meadow is wrapped in shimmering gold ornament in Klimt's signature manner. Painted at the height of the artist's golden period, it became one of the most recognisable images of love in art nouveau.
fact: For the gold ground Klimt used real gold leaf, a nod to the family trade of his goldsmith father.

name: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
description: A portrait of a Viennese society woman, all but dissolved into a mosaic of gold and silver ornament, marked the summit of Klimt's golden period. It has been nicknamed the Austrian Mona Lisa for what it means to the country's art.
fact: The Nazis confiscated the painting from the Bloch-Bauer family, and the heirs only won it back after decades of litigation.

name: Dance
description: Five naked figures hold hands and whirl in a headlong ring against flat planes of blue and green. The extreme simplification of form and the pure saturated colour made it one of the boldest works of European art in the early twentieth century.
fact: It was painted on a commission from the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin, to decorate the staircase of his mansion.

name: Composition VII
description: One of the most complex and largest of Kandinsky's abstract compositions, it pulls echoes of biblical subjects into a whirl of colour: the flood, the resurrection, the last judgement. Before starting, he made dozens of preparatory studies in pursuit of a perfect harmony of colour and form.
fact: Kandinsky painted the enormous canvas itself in only a few days, although he had prepared for it for months.

name: Black Square
description: Malevich regarded this plain black square on a white ground not as decoration but as the zero point of painting: the end of representational art and the birth of suprematism. It was first shown high in the corner of the room where Russian homes traditionally hang their icons.
fact: Malevich made several versions of Black Square himself, and beneath the top layer of paint on the original, traces of earlier compositions have been found.

name: The Son of Man
description: A man in a bowler hat and a formal suit stands against sea and sky, but his face is completely hidden by a hovering green apple. Magritte said it was an image of the endless conflict between the visible and the hidden, between what we want to see and what is kept from us.
fact: The picture is regarded as a kind of self-portrait: Magritte often depicted himself in exactly that bowler hat.

name: The Treachery of Images
meta: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
description: Under a meticulously painted pipe the artist wrote in French "This is not a pipe", reminding the viewer that what is in front of them is only a picture of an object and not the object itself. That paradox made it one of the best known works of surrealism.
fact: Magritte produced several variations of this work under different titles, playing on the same paradox of image and reality.

name: American Gothic
description: A farmer with a pitchfork and his daughter look sternly out at the viewer in front of a plain house in the Gothic style that gave the painting its name. The balanced, almost ironic composition became a defining emblem of conservative rural America and the source of countless parodies.
fact: The models were the artist's sister and his dentist, not an actual farming couple at all.

name: Nighthawks
description: A few late customers sit at the counter of a brightly lit diner on an empty street sunk in darkness. Hopper caught the loneliness and detachment of the big city through the sheer contrast of light and shadow.
fact: Hopper painted it shortly after the attack on Pearl Harbor, and the unease of those months shows in its sombre colour.

name: Christina's World
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: A young woman in a pink dress half reclines in a yellowed meadow, looking towards a distant house on a hill. The model was the artist's neighbour, who had an illness that limited the use of her legs, although nothing in the picture says so directly.
fact: Wyeth painted the landscape and the house from life, and worked up the figure separately, using his own wife as the model for the pose.

name: Campbell's Soup Cans
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Thirty-two identically composed canvases of soup cans in different flavours turned an ordinary supermarket product into a work of art. Warhol chose the subject because he had eaten that brand of soup for lunch almost every day for years.
fact: At the first exhibition the canvases were priced at a hundred dollars each; today the whole series is valued in the tens of millions.

name: Marilyn Diptych
description: Fifty repeating portraits of Marilyn Monroe, split between a vivid colour half and a fading black and white one, made shortly after the actress died. The repetition of a single face hints at how the media turn a living person into an endlessly reproduced image.
fact: Warhol used one and the same publicity still of Monroe, from the film Niagara, as the basis for every portrait.

name: Girl with Balloon
description: The silhouette of a little girl reaching after a red heart-shaped balloon became one of the most recognisable images in Banksy's street art. The simple, touching motif has been reproduced on postcards, T-shirts and posters all over the world.
fact: In 2018 a print of this work was half shredded by a device hidden in its frame right after it sold at auction, and the result was renamed Love is in the Bin.

name: The Two Fridas
meta: Museum of Modern Art, Mexico City
description: The artist painted herself twice over, in European dress with her heart cut open and in a traditional Mexican dress, the two joined by intertwined veins. She painted it shortly after her divorce from Diego Rivera, and it reflects her divided sense of who she was.
fact: This is Frida Kahlo's largest painting, a nearly square canvas about as tall as a person.

name: Whistler's Mother
description: This austere portrait of an elderly woman in a black dress, seated in profile against a plain grey wall, was conceived as a formal exercise in colour and composition. Later it came to be read as a universal image of motherhood and an emblem of America, although it was painted in France.
fact: The work's official title is Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, and only the subtitle mentions that it is the artist's mother.

name: The Ninth Wave
description: After a shipwreck in the night, a handful of survivors cling to the wreckage of a mast among raging waves while the first rays of sun break through the clouds, promising rescue. The title refers to the sailors' belief that the ninth wave in a storm is the most powerful.
fact: Aivazovsky painted the sea almost entirely from memory and imagination, rarely working from life on the shore.

name: Morning in a Pine Forest
description: A she-bear and three cubs play on fallen trunks in the mist of a pine wood at dawn. Shishkin painted the landscape, while the bears were done by the painter Konstantin Savitsky, whose signature was later scrubbed off the canvas at the collector Tretyakov's insistence.
fact: A reproduction of this painting has been the wrapper of a famous Russian chocolate for over a century and is better known than the original itself.

name: The Rooks Have Come Back
description: Newly arrived rooks build their nests in bare birches by a village church, while melting snow and a grey spring sky carry the fragile feeling of nature waking up. This modest, almost everyday subject came to be seen as one of the first truly lyrical Russian landscapes.
fact: Pavel Tretyakov bought the painting for his gallery straight off a travelling exhibition, where it had impressed the critics deeply.

name: Golden Autumn
description: A winding river among golden birches and a yellow field under a bright blue sky catches the short but most colourful season in central Russia. The colour, unusually vivid for Levitan with his normally restrained, melancholy landscapes, made this one of the most recognisable Russian views.
fact: Levitan painted it during a difficult period for him, shortly after his break with the painter Sofia Kuvshinnikova.

name: Above Eternal Peace
description: A small wooden church and its graveyard on a high headland look tiny against an enormous lake and a low, heavy sky. Levitan considered this one of his most personal and philosophical works, a meditation on where a human being stands in the face of eternity.
fact: In his letters the artist admitted that he had put his whole soul and his whole idea of eternity into this picture.

name: Barge Haulers on the Volga
description: Eleven exhausted haulers drag a heavy barge by tow rope through the shallows of the Volga under a blazing sun. Repin travelled to the Volga for several years, studying the haulers' lives and making portrait studies of them before finishing the great canvas.
fact: Among the haulers the artist painted a former priest and a soldier, and one young man stands out for the anger in his eyes amid the submission of the rest.

name: Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan
description: A stricken tsar clutches his mortally wounded son, whom he has just struck with his staff in a fit of rage; the subject follows the half-legendary account of the prince's death. Full of despair and horror, the painting caused a scandal and was banned from display for a time.
fact: The painting has been attacked by vandals several times, including serious damage in 2018, after which it spent years in restoration.
wiki_en: Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan

name: Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks
description: Roaring with laughter, Zaporozhian Cossacks compose an insolent and mocking reply to the Turkish sultan who had demanded their submission. Repin worked on the picture for more than ten years, gathering historical detail of costume and weaponry and making portrait studies from real people.
fact: The huge canvas was bought by Emperor Alexander III in person, for what was then a record sum for a Russian painting.

name: They Did Not Expect Him
description: A gaunt man walks unannounced into a room, by all appearances a political exile come home without warning, and his family freeze in astonishment and joy. Repin caught a whole range of feeling on their faces in this one arrested moment.
fact: The artist repainted the main figure's face several times before he got the expression of half disbelief and hope that he wanted.

name: Boyarynya Morozova
description: The noblewoman Morozova, a schismatic in chains, is carted on a sledge through a crowd of Muscovites, raising two fingers, the Old Believers' sign of the cross. Surikov built a monumental scene of private faith set against the power of the state in the seventeenth century.
fact: For the holy fool sitting in the snow, Surikov made studies from an actual beggar he found at a market, whose expressive face had struck him.

name: The Morning of the Streltsy Execution
description: On Red Square the streltsy condemned to death take leave of their families while they wait for the sentence to be carried out, after the revolt against Peter the Great was crushed. Surikov built a dramatic crowded composition on the contrast between the despair of the condemned and the cold resolve of the young tsar.
fact: Surikov recalled that the idea for the painting came to him from the impression of a candle burning in broad daylight.
wiki_en: The Morning of the Streltsy Execution

name: Taking a Snow Town
description: A rider at full gallop bursts into a snow fortress built for a Shrovetide village game, while all around the crowd laughs and cheers. Unlike his earlier tragic history canvases, here Surikov turned to a bright and joyful scene of Siberian life.
fact: Surikov drew the idea from childhood memories of these games in his native Krasnoyarsk in Siberia.

name: Bogatyrs
description: Three heroes of Russian epic, Ilya Muromets, Dobrynya Nikitich and Alyosha Popovich, sit motionless on their horses, scanning the distance for an enemy on the border of their homeland. Vasnetsov worked on this epic canvas for some twenty years, out to create a monumental image of the defenders of Rus.
fact: Pavel Tretyakov bought the finished canvas at once, and it became one of the centrepieces of his gallery.

name: Alyonushka
description: A sorrowful girl in a plain peasant dress sits on a stone by a dark forest pool with her arms around her knees. The image comes from the Russian folk tale of sister Alyonushka and brother Ivanushka, although the picture does not show that episode directly.
fact: The model for her face was a peasant girl the artist met at the Akhtyrka estate outside Moscow.

name: Ivan Tsarevich Riding the Grey Wolf
description: Ivan Tsarevich races through a dark forest on the back of an enormous grey wolf, carrying off the rescued Yelena the Fair. The painting follows a Russian folk tale and catches the uneasy, fairy-tale mood of a flight through thickets that are in bloom and dangerous at once.
fact: The blossoming apple tree in the middle of the gloomy thicket comes as a surprise and, art historians suggest, stands for hope of a happy ending.

name: The Knight at the Crossroads
description: A lone warrior on horseback has halted before a stone with a half-effaced inscription warning of death down any of the three roads, and the bones of earlier travellers lie scattered around. Vasnetsov built an image of eternal choice and inescapable fate out of a traditional subject from Russian epic.
fact: The artist repainted this picture several times over many years, working towards the bleak mood he wanted in the landscape.

name: The Demon Seated
description: A sorrowful young demon with a powerful torso sits with his arms around his knees among fantastic crystalline flowers against sunset mountains. Vrubel returned to the theme of the Demon, taken from Lermontov's poem, for almost his whole working life, in several paintings and sculptures.
fact: He laid the paint on in small palette-knife strokes, which makes the surface look as though it were built of glowing jewelled facets.

name: The Swan Princess
description: A beautiful maiden with swan's wings glances back over her shoulder against a twilit sea, as if caught for an instant between her two forms. The image comes from Rimsky-Korsakov's opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan, for which Vrubel designed the sets and costumes.
fact: The Swan Princess in that opera was sung by the artist's wife, the singer Nadezhda Zabela-Vrubel, whom Vrubel painted in other works too.

name: Girl with Peaches
description: The young daughter of the patron Savva Mamontov sits at a table with peaches in a sunlit room of the Abramtsevo estate, and light and air seem to fill the entire canvas. Serov painted it all summer long, chasing the sense of a freshness caught on the spot.
fact: The artist was only twenty-two when he worked on this picture, and his model was Vera Mamontova, the daughter of the house.

name: The Rape of Europa
description: The Phoenician princess Europa rides across the sea on the back of the bull into which the enamoured Zeus has turned himself; Serov handled the Greek myth in an almost decorative, generalised manner. Flat bright colour and simplified forms reflect his fascination with archaic art and his journeys to Greece.
fact: Serov made several versions of this subject, including wall panels and graphic studies.

name: Portrait of an Unknown Woman
description: An elegant lady in expensive clothes and a fashionable hat looks down at the viewer from an open carriage against a snowbound Petersburg. Who she was has never been established, which has bred any number of theories about her background and her profession.
fact: Kramskoi's contemporaries argued over whether he had painted a society lady, an actress or a kept woman, and the argument has never died down.

name: The Last Day of Pompeii
description: The people of an ancient city flee through the streets in panic under falling ash and lightning during the eruption of Vesuvius that destroyed Pompeii. The huge canvas brought Bryullov European fame: in Italy and France it was greeted with a triumph rare for a Russian painter.
fact: Bryullov visited the excavations at Pompeii more than once, and some scenes go back to the letters of Pliny the Younger, an eyewitness of the eruption.

name: The Horsewoman
description: A splendidly dressed rider reins in her excited horse in front of a house while a little girl runs out to admire the spectacle. Bryullov painted this formal portrait of Countess Yulia Samoilova's wards in his own lavish, theatrical manner.
fact: An elegant greyhound and a second, smaller dog in the foreground add liveliness and an almost domestic charm to the scene.

name: The Appearance of Christ Before the People
description: John the Baptist points the crowd towards Christ approaching in the distance, and the dozens of figures in the foreground each react to the news in their own way, from rapture to disbelief. Ivanov painted this immense canvas for two decades, after the moment of a spiritual turning point for mankind.
fact: For this painting the artist made hundreds of preparatory studies of heads, figures and landscapes, many of which became valued works in their own right.
wiki_en: The Appearance of Christ Before the People

name: The Trinity
meta: transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church
description: Three angels sit in thoughtful silence at a table around a cup, standing for the Christian Trinity through the soft rhythm of the lines and a muted gold and blue palette. The icon is regarded as the summit of old Russian icon painting and one of the most perfect works of religious art anywhere.
fact: It was painted for the Trinity Lavra of St Sergius in memory of the abbot Sergius of Radonezh, and in 2023 it was handed over to the Russian Orthodox Church.

name: The Apotheosis of War
description: A mountain of skulls lies in the middle of a scorched desert, and the crows circling above it are the only living things in sight. Vereshchagin dedicated the picture to all great conquerors, past, present and to come, which makes it one of the most forceful anti-war statements in painting.
fact: The work closes Vereshchagin's Turkestan series and draws on accounts of the pyramids of skulls that Tamerlane had built.

name: Hunters at Rest
description: Three hunters have stopped for a rest after the shoot, and one of them is telling an obviously tall story with great enthusiasm while his companions listen in frank disbelief. Perov caught a situation everybody knows, the hunter's tale, with fine irony in the poses and faces.
fact: Perov was a passionate hunter himself, so he painted the scene from his own experience, using acquaintances as models.

name: Troika
description: Three exhausted peasant children drag a heavy sledge with an iced-up water barrel through the snow, pushing on against a blizzard with the last of their strength. A troika normally means a team of three horses; here Perov gave the name to the children harnessed to the sledge in place of draught animals.
fact: Years later the mother of the boy who posed for the central figure came to Perov, and he painted her a separate portrait of her son; the picture itself already belonged to Tretyakov.

name: The Unequal Marriage
description: An elderly rich bridegroom slips a ring onto the finger of a pale young bride while behind them the young best man watches the wedding with bitter resentment. The painting became a landmark indictment of the marriages of convenience common in merchant and gentry circles in the nineteenth century.
fact: By one account the artist painted himself as the unhappy best man, hinting at a love of his own that came to nothing.

name: Another Bad Mark
description: A schoolboy comes in at the door with his satchel looking guilty, and the disappointed looks of his mother, his sister and his little brother with the dog make it plain at once that he has brought home another bad mark. This simple scene of Soviet school life became one of the most reproduced pictures of its time.
fact: Reproductions of this painting were printed in school textbooks and on postcards across the Soviet Union for decades.

name: Bathing of a Red Horse
description: A naked youth on an enormous scarlet horse rises above still water, and the horse itself looks more like a symbol than a real animal. The unexpected, saturated colour of the horse and the almost icon-like composition made the picture feel like a premonition of the upheavals to come in Russian history.
fact: Many contemporaries later read the scarlet horse as a prophecy of revolution and war, though the picture was painted before those events.

name: Merchant's Wife at Tea
description: A plump, rosy-cheeked merchant's wife takes her tea unhurriedly on a balcony, with a watermelon, fruit and a samovar on the table and a provincial Russian town behind her. Kustodiev painted this while already gravely ill, from memory of pre-war merchant life, giving the scene an almost fairy-tale festivity.
fact: The model for her face was a neighbour from the artist's flat in Petrograd, although Kustodiev noticeably embellished her figure.

name: Moscow Courtyard
description: A sunny summer courtyard with children playing, hens about and an old church behind conveys the simple, comfortable life of old Moscow. The light, almost sketch-like handling made this small intimate picture one of the best loved images in Russian landscape painting.
fact: Polenov painted this courtyard straight from the window of his rented flat in Moscow, where he had returned after some years abroad.

name: Moonlit Night on the Dnieper
description: A mysterious greenish moonlight is reflected in the calm water of the Dnieper, while the dark Ukrainian cottages are barely visible in the gloom. The unusual brightness of that glow so astonished the public at the first showing that many suspected the artist of using special, almost luminous paints.
fact: It was shown in what was then an unheard-of one-painting exhibition, in a darkened room under directed light, and enormous queues formed at the door.

name: Birch Grove
description: The bright trunks of white birches are lit by the midday sun against the deep shade of the forest, and the tops of the trees are cut off by the frame. The stark, almost decorative play of light and shade made this one of the boldest works of colour in nineteenth-century Russian landscape.
fact: Kuindzhi deliberately simplified and generalised the detail of the landscape, for which his contemporaries often accused him of excessive decorativeness.

name: The Major's Marriage Proposal
description: A merchant's house is in uproar: the major who has come to propose waits in the next room while the flustered bride tries to flee at the last moment and her mother holds her back by the dress. Fedotov drew with fine humour the marriage for money and a noble title so common in merchant circles.
fact: The artist was himself a retired officer and took an ironic view of the typical manners and class prejudices of his day.

name: Dogs Playing Poker
description: A series of comic paintings by the American artist Cassius Coolidge in which anthropomorphic dogs play cards, smoke and drink around a table. They were made as advertising for a cigar company and had no pretensions to high art. Over time the series became a byword for kitsch American humour.
fact: The paintings were commissioned by a cigar and tobacco firm for advertising calendars, and not as art in their own right.

name: The Potato Eaters
description: One of van Gogh's first major works, painted in a dark earthy range and showing a peasant family at a meagre supper. He wanted to show working people exactly as they were, honestly and without flattery. Van Gogh himself considered it the most important achievement of his early years.
fact: Van Gogh wrote that he wanted to show how these people had honestly earned their humble food with the very hands that dug the earth.

name: Wheatfield with Crows
description: An uneasy landscape with a turbulent sky, a ploughed field and a flock of black crows rising over the ears of wheat. It was painted shortly before the artist's death and is often read as a foreboding of the end, though it is not his last work. The harsh strokes and dark palette carry the inner tension of the late van Gogh.
fact: Despite the widespread belief, this was not van Gogh's final painting before his death.

name: Irises
description: A vivid flower piece painted soon after van Gogh admitted himself voluntarily to the asylum at Saint-Rémy. The saturated blues and violets of the irises against orange earth set up an almost decorative, energetic rhythm. The artist himself thought of the work as a study rather than a finished painting.
fact: In 1987 the painting sold at auction for what was then a record sum, setting a new benchmark for prices in painting.

name: Bedroom in Arles
description: The artist's own bedroom in the yellow house at Arles, painted in simple flat planes of colour. Van Gogh wanted the bright, contrasting tones themselves to express calm and rest. He cared so much for the subject that he made two further versions of the picture.
fact: Van Gogh painted three nearly identical versions of this bedroom, differing slightly in details and shades.

name: The Milkmaid
description: An intimate scene: a servant pours milk into an earthenware jug by a kitchen window, wholly absorbed in the task. The soft window light and the careful rendering of bread, cloth and crockery make the picture a model of Dutch golden-age domestic painting. Vermeer turned an ordinary chore into an almost solemn composition.
fact: Research has shown that the wall behind the woman originally carried an image, which Vermeer later painted over, leaving the wall bare.

name: View of Delft
description: A panoramic view of Vermeer's native city, painted from the far bank of the canal in the particular light that follows rain. The artist rendered the play of light on roofs, water and clouds with almost photographic precision. It is counted among the finest cityscapes in the history of painting.
fact: Marcel Proust thought this the most beautiful painting in the world and gave it lines in his novel.

name: The Triumph of Death
description: An apocalyptic panorama in which an army of skeletons destroys people of every rank against a scorched, lifeless earth. The dense, detail-packed composition echoes the horrors of plague and war that Europe knew well at the time. It remains one of the bleakest and most detailed images of death in the history of art.
fact: Dozens of separate scenes of people dying can be counted in the picture, from nobles to peasants: nobody is spared.

name: The Parable of the Blind
description: Six blind beggars walk in single file, each with a hand on the shoulder of the man in front, and the first is already falling into a ditch, pulling the rest after him. The painting illustrates the gospel parable of the blind leading the blind, a bitter reflection on human ignorance. Every figure is painted with medical precision.
fact: The blindness is rendered in such detail that doctors were later able to identify each beggar's particular eye disease from the painting.

name: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus
meta: attributed to Pieter Bruegel the Elder
description: At first glance an ordinary rural landscape with a ploughman, a shepherd and a fisherman, and only in the corner do the drowning legs of Icarus stick out of the water, unnoticed by any of them. The composition makes the point that great disasters often pass unremarked amid everyday life. Its authorship is disputed.
fact: Most art historians today regard the picture not as an original Bruegel but as a later copy of a work that has not survived.
wiki_en: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus

name: The Sleeping Gypsy
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: A mysterious night scene: a sleeping woman lies on bare ground while a lion stands beside her, sniffing at her but doing her no harm. The naive, almost childlike manner of Rousseau, a self-taught painter, creates a waking-dream atmosphere between reality and fantasy. He offered the picture to the town of Laval and was turned down.
fact: Rousseau, who had no training in art, painted this scene by combining realistic detail with a frankly unreal, fairy-tale atmosphere.

name: The Dream
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Rousseau's last large painting: a naked woman reclines on a sofa in the middle of lush jungle, among lions, birds and a snake charmer. The artist explained that the sofa had been carried into the forest in the sleeping woman's dream. The riotous foliage is painted with almost ornamental care, although Rousseau never left France.
fact: Rousseau never visited the tropics and painted his exotic plants on the strength of visits to the Paris botanical garden.

name: Harmony in Red
description: An interior flooded almost entirely with saturated red, which erases the boundary between wall and table and turns the room into a single ornamental space. Matisse repainted the picture, first conceived in blue, changing its whole colour before finishing. It counts as a high point of fauvism.
fact: Matisse first painted this same composition in blue tones under the title Harmony in Blue, then repainted it completely in red.

name: The Weeping Woman
description: A portrait of a woman whose face is distorted and broken into cubist planes, her tears rendered in sharp, almost cutting lines. The painting carries on from Guernica and reflects the tragedy of the Spanish Civil War. The model was the photographer and artist Dora Maar, Picasso's companion in those years.
fact: The model was Dora Maar, a photographer and artist who was Picasso's close friend and muse for several years.

name: Acrobat on a Ball
description: A fragile acrobat balances on a ball opposite a massive strongman sitting perfectly still: a contrast of movement and stasis, lightness and weight. The painting belongs to Picasso's so-called rose period, tied to the world of travelling circus performers. It came into a Russian collection before the revolution.
fact: The businessman and patron Ivan Morozov bought the painting for his Moscow collection before the First World War.

name: Three Musicians
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: Three figures in commedia dell'arte masks, a Harlequin, a Pierrot and a monk, are packed into a dense cubist composition of bright flat shapes of colour. Picasso made two nearly identical versions of this picture in the same period. It counts as a high point of his synthetic cubism.
fact: Picasso painted two almost identical versions of this composition at once, and they now hang in different museums.

name: Boy with a Pipe
description: A portrait of a Parisian youth wearing a wreath of flowers and holding a pipe, painted in the soft rosy range of Picasso's early years. It belongs to the rose period that followed the darker blue one. In the early twenty-first century the work set one of the auction records for painting.
fact: In 2004 the painting sold at auction for almost 105 million dollars, then one of the highest prices ever paid for a picture.

name: Composition with Red, Yellow and Blue
description: A severe abstract composition of straight black lines and rectangular blocks of pure red, yellow and blue on white. Mondrian reduced painting to the simplest possible elements, seeking to express a universal harmony through geometry and primary colours. He made several variants of this kind over the years.
fact: In his mature years Mondrian limited his palette to black, white, grey and the three primary colours, which he saw as pure harmony.
wiki_en: Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow

name: The Lovers
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: A couple kiss through heavy cloth that completely covers both their faces, so that an intimate gesture turns into an image of estrangement and of closeness made impossible. Magritte painted several versions of this subject with heads wrapped in cloth. It became one of the most recognisable images of surrealism.
fact: Several versions of this painting exist with cloth over the lovers' heads, differing in background and in details of the composition.

name: The Empire of Light
description: A paradoxical landscape in which a night street with lit lamps and houses sits below a clear daytime sky. Magritte called this quiet but disquieting mismatch of light and darkness poetic and mysterious at once. He made more than a dozen variants of the composition in oil and gouache.
fact: The various versions of The Empire of Light are scattered across the world's museums, in New York, Venice and Brussels among others.

name: Oath of the Horatii
description: The three Horatii brothers swear to their father that they will fight to the death for Rome, stretching their arms towards the swords he holds up, while the women of the family stand frozen in grief to one side. The severe composition and the classical subject made it the manifesto of neoclassicism in French painting.
fact: It was painted shortly before the French Revolution and read by many contemporaries as a call to civic virtue.

name: The Death of Marat
description: The revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat lies dead in his bath, where the assassin Charlotte Corday found him; the pose and the lighting deliberately recall paintings of the lamentation over Christ. David, Marat's friend and a witness of the revolution, painted it almost immediately after the murder.
fact: Marat suffered from a skin disease and worked for long stretches sitting in a medicinal bath, which is exactly where his killer found him.

name: Napoleon Crossing the Alps
description: Napoleon is shown on a rearing horse, pointing forward as he crosses an Alpine pass, although in reality he crossed the mountains on a mule in far humbler circumstances. David created a heroic, almost mythological image of the future emperor; the first version was commissioned by King Charles IV of Spain.
fact: Napoleon actually crossed the pass on the back of a mule, not on the rearing horse so strikingly shown in the painting.

name: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp
description: A group portrait of Amsterdam surgeons gathered around Dr Tulp during a public anatomical dissection. Rembrandt brought the conventional group portrait to life by giving each man his own expression of attention and curiosity. It was one of the first works to make the young artist widely known.
fact: Anatomy lessons of this kind were public events at the time and mattered a great deal in the life of the Amsterdam surgeons' guild.
wiki_en: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp

name: The Return of the Prodigal Son
description: One of Rembrandt's last and most piercing works: an almost blind father embraces his gaunt son, kneeling before him, while witnesses stand silent in the shadows. A soft warm light picks the gesture of forgiveness out of the darkness. He painted it in his final years, after personal loss and poverty.
fact: Art historians note that the father's hands are painted differently, one looking male and the other female, and read this as fatherly and motherly love combined.
wiki_en: The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt)

name: Haystacks
description: A series of more than twenty paintings showing the same haystack at different times of day and year: at sunset, in snow, in mist. What interested Monet was not the hay so much as the changing light and atmosphere around a motionless object. The series was a key impressionist experiment with effects of light.
fact: Monet worked on several canvases at once, moving his brushes from one to another as the light changed through the day.

name: Rouen Cathedral
description: A series of more than thirty paintings of one and the same facade of Rouen Cathedral, caught under different light, from dawn haze to bright midday sun. Monet rented a room opposite the cathedral and worked on several canvases in parallel through the day, showing how one motif can look wholly different.
fact: Monet showed twenty paintings from this series together at a Paris exhibition in 1895.

name: Woman with a Parasol
description: A portrait of the artist's wife Camille out walking with their son, painted in light, almost airy strokes and seen from below, so that the figure seems to float against a cloudy sky. Wind, light and movement are carried by the free, dynamic brushwork of impressionism.
fact: The models were the artist's wife Camille Monet and their son Jean, standing a little behind her on the hill.
wiki_en: Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son

name: Luncheon of the Boating Party
description: A party of the artist's friends has settled on the terrace of a riverside restaurant after boating, in a scene full of light, wine and the easy pleasure of Parisian life in the late nineteenth century. Among the guests Renoir painted his future wife Aline Charigot, playing with a little dog in the foreground.
fact: Among the guests Renoir painted his future wife Aline Charigot: she sits on the left with a small dog in her arms.

name: The Swing
description: A playful rococo scene: a young woman soars on a swing pushed by an older man in the shade, while an admirer hidden in the bushes looks up her skirt and a slipper flies off her foot. The light, flirtatious composition was commissioned by that very admirer.
fact: By the surviving accounts, the painting was commissioned by the hidden admirer shown in it, who wanted to see himself beside his beloved's swing.

name: Mont Sainte-Victoire
description: A lone mountain in the south of France that Cézanne painted dozens of times over many years, chasing not literal likeness but the inner structure of the landscape in planes and volumes. These late works largely anticipated the rise of cubism. The mountain stood near his home at Aix-en-Provence.
fact: Cézanne painted this mountain so often and so long that his method of analysing form through geometric planes shaped the birth of cubism.

name: The Card Players
description: A series of five paintings of peasants absorbed in a game of cards at a plain table, their still figures rendered with almost sculptural weight and calm. Cézanne stripped the scene of all the theatricality and anecdote that earlier pictures of card players had carried.
fact: In 2011 one version of the painting was sold privately for around 250 million dollars, at the time one of the highest prices in the history of painting.

name: At the Moulin Rouge
description: A night scene in a Paris cabaret: a group of regulars sits at a table while in the foreground a woman's face appears in harsh green light, looking almost like a mask. Toulouse-Lautrec was a regular at the Moulin Rouge and knew the people he painted. The boldly cropped composition owes much to Japanese prints.
fact: Most of the figures are real regulars of the cabaret, acquaintances of the artist, including Toulouse-Lautrec himself at the back.

name: The Last Judgment
description: A vast fresco on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel showing Christ at the Last Judgement, with the righteous rising and the damned falling around him in a whirl of bodies. Michelangelo painted the nudes with a boldness unheard of in church art, which scandalised his contemporaries.
fact: After Michelangelo's death the church authorities had another artist paint draperies over the nude figures that had caused so much argument.

name: Portrait of Dr Gachet
description: A portrait of the physician Paul Gachet, who looked after van Gogh in the last months of his life at Auvers; the pensive pose and melancholy gaze of the sitter echo the state of the artist himself. Van Gogh made two versions of this portrait shortly before his death.
fact: In 1990 the portrait sold at auction for a record sum that remained among the highest in the history of art sales for decades.

name: Starry Night Over the Rhône
description: A night view of the Rhône at Arles, with the lights of the town reflected in the dark water and a starry sky blazing above them. Unlike the later Starry Night in New York, this is a real and recognisable landscape, painted from life in the evening. The shimmering strokes give the sky a breathing life.
fact: Van Gogh painted this night view out on the embankment under the open sky, not from memory in the studio.

name: I and the Village
meta: Museum of Modern Art, New York
description: A fantastic composition in which the huge head of an animal and the face of a peasant look at each other, while houses, trees and people from Chagall's native Vitebsk circle around them. The artist fused childhood memory with cubist devices into an almost dreamlike image.
fact: The composition rests on Chagall's childhood memories of his native Vitebsk and of Jewish small-town life.

name: Over the Town
description: A couple in love floats through the air above the roofs of a provincial town much like Chagall's native Vitebsk; he used the motif of flight in many works as a symbol of love and freedom. The models for the pair were Chagall himself and his wife Bella.
fact: In the painting the artist showed himself together with his wife Bella, floating over the roofs of their native Vitebsk.

name: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
description: Manet's last major painting: a barmaid at a Paris cabaret stands behind a counter of bottles and fruit, and the mirror behind her reflects the hall with its customers, though the reflection does not obey the laws of optics. That deliberate mismatch has occupied art historians for decades.
fact: The reflection in the mirror behind the barmaid does not match the real positions of the figures at the counter, and the discrepancy is still argued over.

name: The Vladimirka Road
description: An empty road runs off to the horizon under a low overcast sky. At first glance an ordinary landscape, but the title points to the notorious route along which convicts were driven to Siberia for centuries. Levitan made not a view of a place but an image of a nation's grief set in a quiet countryside.
fact: Along the Vladimirka road shown here, convicts were marched on foot to Siberia for centuries, which gives the landscape its mournful meaning.

name: March
description: A sunny spring landscape with melting snow by the porch of a village house, where a horse waits patiently for its owner and the branches already stir with early spring. The bright light and ringing colour stand out sharply from the restrained, melancholy manner of much of Levitan's other work.
fact: This is considered one of the brightest and most optimistic canvases by Levitan, who is known above all for melancholy landscapes.

name: Autumn Day. Sokolniki
description: One of the first major works by the young Levitan: a solitary female figure walks along an avenue in Sokolniki park among trees shedding their autumn leaves. The quiet, piercing melancholy of this picture already points towards the mood landscapes he would later make his own.
fact: By the common account, the woman on the avenue was painted in not by Levitan but by his fellow student Nikolai Chekhov, the writer's brother.

name: By the Whirlpool
description: A sombre landscape with a wooden footbridge over a dark pool in twilight, steeped in local stories of unhappy fates and drowned girls. According to contemporaries, the choice of subject was prompted by a real estate connected with a tragic legend. The thick, almost viscous mood makes it one of his most troubling works.
fact: The subject is tied to a local legend about a drowned woman that Levitan heard while working on studies in central Russia.

name: Portrait of Alexander Pushkin
description: One of the best known portraits made of Alexander Pushkin in his lifetime, showing the poet as a dreamer with his arms folded across his chest and a bronze muse with a lyre over his shoulder. It was commissioned by Pushkin's close friend Anton Delvig.
fact: In response to this portrait Pushkin dedicated a poem to Kiprensky, thanking him for the image he had created.

name: Religious Procession in Kursk Province
description: A crowded panorama of a religious procession carrying an icon along a dusty road, in which Repin showed the whole range of Russian society of his day with almost documentary precision, from beggars and cripples to officials and prosperous peasants. The dense, motley crowd was his way of speaking about inequality.
fact: In the crowd of pilgrims Repin painted people of every estate, from crippled beggars to rich merchants and policemen, an almost sociological cross-section.

name: The Demon Downcast
description: The defeated winged demon lies among sharp mountain crags, his body broken and twisted and his gaze fixed: the last and darkest part of Vrubel's demon cycle. The artist kept repainting the picture even during exhibitions, driving himself to nervous exhaustion.
fact: Vrubel went on repainting the picture after the exhibition had opened, in the gallery itself in front of visitors, which alarmed those close to him.

name: The Snow Maiden
description: A fragile girl in a white fur coat stands at the edge of a winter forest against dark trees and the distant lights of a village: a fairy-tale image Vasnetsov made under the impression of designing sets for an opera on the same story. He worked a great deal for the theatre in those years.
fact: The painting grew out of Vasnetsov's work on theatre sets and costumes for a production of the same fairy tale.

name: After the Battle of Igor Svyatoslavich with the Polovtsians
description: The field after a battle between the Russian army and the Polovtsians is strewn with the bodies of the fallen under an uneasy sunset sky; the subject is taken from The Tale of Igor's Campaign. Vasnetsov deliberately gave up the drama of battle for a quiet, almost epic mourning of the dead.
fact: The subject comes from The Tale of Igor's Campaign, one of the oldest surviving works of Russian literature.
wiki_ru: После побоища Игоря Святославича с половцами

name: The Vision of the Youth Bartholomew
description: A boy named Bartholomew, the future Sergius of Radonezh, meets a mysterious hermit at the edge of a wood: a quiet, almost silent scene against a piercingly delicate Russian landscape. Nesterov painted the setting from life near Abramtsevo, not far from the Trinity Lavra of St Sergius.
fact: The youth Bartholomew in the painting is the future Sergius of Radonezh, one of the most revered of Russian saints.

name: The Defence of Sevastopol
description: A dramatic scene of hand-to-hand fighting between Soviet sailors and German soldiers against a ruined city, painted at the height of the war with Nazi Germany and charged with an almost poster-like force. The harsh, contrasting silhouettes in the foreground sharpen the tension of the fight.
fact: The painting was made in 1942, in the middle of the war, and was conceived from the outset as a large heroic work to lift morale.

name: Rest After Battle
description: A group of Soviet soldiers gathered around a joker during a short halt laughs together at his story; the subject echoes the figure of Vasily Tyorkin from Alexander Tvardovsky's poem. The warm, everyday scene contrasts with the harshness of wartime, of which only the background reminds us.
fact: The central figure deliberately recalls Vasily Tyorkin, the soldier hero of Alexander Tvardovsky's famous poem.

name: The Fresh Cavalier
description: A hung-over civil servant struts about an untidy room in the morning in his dressing gown, proudly showing off his newly awarded decoration to the cook: a caustic satire on petty vanity and the worship of rank. Fedotov, a founder of genre painting in Russia, filled the scene with telling detail.
fact: The painting has a second, longer title: The Morning of an Official Who Has Received His First Decoration.

name: An Aristocrat's Breakfast
description: An impoverished dandy hastily covers a modest piece of black bread on a tray with a book at the sound of an unexpected visitor: the scene mocks showy luxury kept up on an empty purse. Fedotov paints the room with irony and an eye for the small remnants of a former prosperity.
fact: The dandy in the painting is hurrying to hide his humble breakfast, passing himself off as a far wealthier man than he is.

name: Home for the Holidays
description: A boy in the dress uniform of a Suvorov military school comes home for the holidays and the whole family greets him joyfully at the door: a warm genre scene of Soviet post-war life, full of familiar domestic detail. It continues Reshetnikov's series of works about childhood and family.
fact: The picture became so popular that reproductions of it were printed in school textbooks and on postcards throughout the USSR.

name: Morning
description: A bright scene full of morning sun: a schoolgirl does her exercises in a room flooded with light before the day begins. The model was the artist's own daughter. The simple, life-affirming subject and the clear, airy painting made this one of the best loved works of Soviet art.
fact: The model for the girl was the artist's own daughter Elena, shown in their family flat.

name: Haymaking
description: Peasants cut tall summer grass in a sunlit meadow: a joyful, light-filled scene painted right after the end of the war as a hymn to peaceful work and a return to ordinary life. Plastov, who painted village life all his career, rendered it in bright, almost impressionist strokes.
fact: The painting was made immediately after the war ended and was seen by contemporaries as a symbol of the return to peaceful life.

name: Rainbow
description: A broad steppe panorama with a vivid rainbow over a field after rain; Kuindzhi, famous for his attention to effects of light, worked here towards an almost luminous saturation of colour. He experimented with the make-up of his paints, chasing the natural radiance of daylight.
fact: For many years Kuindzhi showed almost no new work in public, while he went on experimenting privately with effects of light in his studio.

name: Christ in the Wilderness
description: A solitary figure of Christ sits on a stone in a bare rocky desert, sunk in heavy thought before the ministry ahead of him. Kramskoi painted not a gospel miracle but a moment of agonising moral choice that any person can understand. He considered this his chief and hardest-won work.
fact: Kramskoi himself called this painting his main creation, one whose idea he had turned over in his mind for many years.

name: Inconsolable Grief
description: A woman in black mourning dress stands frozen by a child's coffin with a handkerchief pressed to her face; the restrained, almost static composition conveys the numbness of unbearable loss. The dark palette and the rigid pose make the grief almost tangible, without a single superfluous gesture.
fact: Kramskoi's own loss of two small sons largely determined the deeply personal character of this painting.

name: Menshikov in Berezovo
description: Alexander Menshikov, Peter the Great's disgraced companion, sits in a cramped hut in Siberian exile among his children, sunk in heavy thoughts of his former power and his present fall. Surikov caught the tightness of the hut and the contrast between the massive, imperious figure and the squalid surroundings.
fact: The low hut is so cramped that Menshikov's figure looks as though it barely fits the room, which sharpens the humiliation of the fallen grandee.
